extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students studying projective/analytic geometry and numerical trigonometric computation
extracted.subtask_description: The page presents 19th‑century mathematical theory and procedures: (1) algebraic theory of collineation between coordinate systems (definitions, equations, special loci like collinear centre, collinear axis, collinear cutis, counter axis, and their algebraic conditions); and (2) numerical algorithms and tables for computing tangents and antitangents (arctangents), including decomposition methods and convergence/precision rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for two systems to be collinearly related (coordinate transformation form)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relations between coordinates of corresponding points of two coUinearly related systems can be expressed by equations of the form (4) (derived from (3) after removing origins and transforming axes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text shows how, after removing origins and possibly rotating axes, the transformation between systems {xy} and {tu} reduces to rational linear forms (see equations (3), (a), (a') leading to (4)). These equations are the working criterion: when coordinates satisfy these forms (with appropriate constants m, n, p, etc.), the systems are coUinearly related. The derivation includes substitutions to simplify constants (see articles III–IV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collinear centre (collinear point)
rubrics_metrics.description: The new origin of a system obtained by choosing axes through the common collinear point is termed the collinear centre (or collinear point) of that system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By translating axes so that the common collinear point is the origin, the coordinate relations simplify to the canonical forms (eqs. (4)). Each coUinearly related system in general has only one collinear point (unless special parameter values allow interchangeability). The collinear centre is the point through which corresponding lines coincide when the systems are superposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collinear axis (equation and special cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: The collinear axis is the straight line (in the system {xy} or {tu}) determined by the equation derived from the transformation constants; e.g. in general forms from (4), and in special cases specific equations such as (10) my + nx = 0 (when β = 1) or (11) my + nx + 2 = 0 (when β = −1) arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The collinear axis is the locus in one system where corresponding lines of the two systems intersect. The exact algebraic form depends on constants (m,n,p, β). The page gives how to compute the equation of the collinear axis from the transformation constants and discusses geometric significance and distances from the collinear centre in special parameter cases (see §§VI–VII and equations (10)–(14)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collinear cutis (locus of coincident corresponding points)
rubrics_metrics.description: If corresponding points coincide (t = x and u = y), besides the collinear point(s) all points of the straight line given by equation (7): my + nx + 1 − p = 0 coincide with their corresponding points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve the transformation equations with t = x and u = y; the resulting condition yields the collinear cutis (equation (7)). The text names this line and explains that every line of one system intersects its corresponding line of the other system in the collinear axis (the cutis gives additional coincident points besides the collinear centre).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter axis (locus of intersections corresponding to parallel lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: The locus of the intersections of corresponding lines in one system that come from parallel lines in the other system is a straight line called the counter axis, with equation given (for {xy}) by (8): my + nx + 1 = 0 (and an analogous equation for {tu} given by (9)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given two parallel lines in system {tu}, their corresponding lines in {xy} generally intersect; the locus of those intersections is the counter axis (equation (8)). The text describes how to compute the counter axis from transformation constants (see §VI) and notes special coincidences of counter and collinear axes in parameter cases (e.g. β = −1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of parallel lines under collineation (non‑preservation of parallelism)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two straight lines of one system are parallel, the lines corresponding to them in the other system are, in general, not parallel; their intersections form a straight line parallel to the collinear axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page demonstrates with equations (a) and the transformed forms (4) that images of parallel lines intersect except when a specific parameter (p i) equals zero; it identifies the intersection locus and relates it to the collinear axis and counter axis (see §VI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchangeability of corresponding points when β = −1
rubrics_metrics.description: When β = −1 (a special parameter value), the coordinates of corresponding points are the same in both systems and any number of corresponding points may be interchanged between systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text shows that for β = −1 the transformed coordinate expressions coincide so that x = t and y = u for corresponding points; consequences include multiple incidence properties and coincidence of counter axes and collinear axes under this special condition (see §VII and equations (11)–(14)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: remove origins and rotate axes to simplify collineation equations
rubrics_metrics.description: To simplify the general transformation equations, remove the origins by substitutions t + t', u + u', x + x', y + y' and, if needed, rotate axes via x cos θ − y sin θ, x sin θ + y cos θ to reduce constants and achieve canonical forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article III demonstrates detailed algebraic manipulations (substitutions and rotations) that reduce the general forms (3) to simpler canonical equations (4) and related conditions (7), (7'). These steps are the recommended method to algebraically normalize a collineation for study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of series and decomposition to compute antitangents (arctangents)
rubrics_metrics.description: For computing antitangents tan⁻¹ x, use the series tan⁻¹ x = x − x^3/3 + x^5/5 − ... (formula (1)), but for values of x near unity this series converges slowly; therefore decompose the number into a sum of smaller quotients whose arctangents are readily found from tables and summed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The algorithm (arts. 2–5) prescribes: divide the target number a by denominators b1, b2,... choosing each quotient r_i restricted to one significant figure (or until r_i begins with p ciphers), iteratively decompose a into a sum of values whose arctangents are small and listed in the provided tables (Table III). Then tan⁻¹ a ≈ sum of tan⁻¹ r_i + small remainder tan⁻¹ m, with rigorous control of precision. The author also recommends using addition formulas tan⁻¹ u + tan⁻¹ v for reconstructing arctangents when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm for practical decomposition to achieve target precision
rubrics_metrics.description: To find tan⁻¹ a to p decimal places: repeatedly divide a by chosen divisors and take one‑figure quotients r_i until the quotient begins with at least p ciphers; then tan⁻¹ a ≈ tan⁻¹ r1 + tan⁻¹ r2 + ... + tan⁻¹ rn + tan⁻¹ m, where m is the final small remainder whose arctangent is directly approximable to p places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles 2–4 explain the iterative division process and the stopping criterion (quotient begins with p ciphers). The values of tan⁻¹ r_i are read from Table III (second and third columns for circular measure and degrees). For degree answers, convert circular‑measure remainders appropriately using π/180 (Table I) and Table II for multiples if needed. The method leverages that when m begins with p leading zeros, tan⁻¹ m truncated gives the required p‑place accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precomputed tables and constants
rubrics_metrics.description: The method requires Table I (multiples of π/180), Table II (multiples of 57.295779...), Table III (values of tan and corresponding antitangents in circular measure and degrees), and the constant π/180 ≈ 0.017453292519943296.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles 1–3 enumerate the auxiliary tables and constants to be preprepared. The tables supply tan⁻¹ values for a grid of small rational arguments (the r_i used in decomposition). The constant π/180 is used to convert between circular measure and degrees when computing or tabulating remainders and final results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series vs. decomposition: when to use which
rubrics_metrics.description: Use direct power‑series expansion tan⁻¹ x = x − x^3/3 + ... to compute antitangents for small x (fast convergence); for x approaching unity, use decomposition into sums of arguments whose arctangents are in tables and combine via addition formulas because the series converges slowly near |x| ≈ 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 2 explicitly notes poor convergence of the arctangent series near unity and prescribes decomposition/compound addition methods for that range; the tables and iterative quotienting provide the practical workaround. The text gives methods to compute the sequence of decomposed r_i efficiently (arts. 3–5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm for computing tangent from an arc
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute tan a given arc a (< π/2), express a as a sum of known table arcs: a = tan⁻¹ r1 + tan⁻¹ r2 + ... + tan⁻¹ rn + tan⁻¹ m, then use addition formulae to compute tan a from the sequence of tan values (art. 7–9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: select nearest tabulated antitangents less than the target arc; iterate remainders until sufficiently small; then combine the tabulated tan values using the tangent addition relations (the algebraic process for computing intermediate b_i and C_i is detailed in art. 9). For arcs given in degrees convert to circular measure (use Table I) as needed. For angles > π/2 use cotangent relations (art. 10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision bookkeeping and conversion between measures
rubrics_metrics.description: When targeting p decimal places, ensure remainders or quotients begin with at least p significant leading zeros (ciphers) in circular measure; when reporting in degrees, convert remainders by multiplying by 180/π (use Table I/II) — precision in circular measure roughly corresponds to p×(π/180) in degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles 2, 3, and 7 emphasize stopping criteria based on leading digits and how to obtain p‑place accuracy. The text warns about conversions: if m is the small circular‑measure remainder, m•(180/π) gives degrees; use Table II for conversion factors. The author notes approximate relation of decimal places between circular measure and degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross‑order multiplication scheme for computing decomposition quotients (r_i) and combination coefficients (b_i, c_i)
rubrics_metrics.description: The computation of successive quotients r_i (and the analogous b_i, c_i when reconstructing tangents) is done by a cross‑multiplication arrangement: r_i = (b_i + a_i − b_i r_{i−1}) / b_{i−1} etc., with explicit tabular column operations shown in arts. 4 and 9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page provides explicit columnar arithmetic prescriptions for efficient hand computation: multiplying in cross order so that quantities from the second column multiply the r_j in the first column to yield addends, etc. Follow the described column procedures to avoid recomputing entire products repeatedly when iterating decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of algebraic division principle to derive differential and transform formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: Many differential and algebraic transformation formulae arise from the principle of transformation by division by unity (stopping the division one term earlier in successive courses), allowing derivation of finite difference relations, Taylor's theorem, and other transformation identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the discussion (arts. 40–47) the author explains a unifying algebraic division viewpoint: altering how far division continues yields the usual differential formulae and finite difference relations. This is presented as a methodological standard for deriving transformation and series relations in analysis (e.g., generating binomial theorem and formulas linking transformee terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical note: prefer finite‑difference route for binomial and related theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: The author recommends deriving the Binomial Theorem and similar results via finite differences because it uses minimal material and yields simple, satisfactory bases for transformation theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a methodological recommendation (scholium) arguing that the finite‑difference approach is economical and elegant for deducing standard analysis theorems; it indicates a choice of method rather than a hard constraint.
